chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Ibn Muskhan from Muhammad al-Halabi said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about al-salam (advance payment for goods) in food measured by a known volume for a known period. He said, 'There is no objection to it.'

key_terms.إِلَى أَجَلٍ مَعْلُوم: For a known period (referring to the delivery time being clearly defined)
key_terms.اَلسَّلَم: Salam (a specific type of sale where payment is made in advance for goods delivered later)
key_terms.اَلطَّعَام: Food (specifically referring to staple foodstuffs in this context)
key_terms.بِكَيْلٍ مَعْلُوم: By a known measure (referring to the quantity being clearly defined)
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no objection to it (a legal ruling indicating permissibility)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to buy food with advance payment for future delivery in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from Sahih al-Tusi confirms the validity of 'bay' al-salam' (advance payment for goods), a crucial commercial mechanism in early Islamic finance that mitigated risk for producers. The Imam’s concise ruling of 'la ba's bihi' (no objection) underscores the permissibility of fixed terms for both quantity and delivery time, provided the essential elements of the contract are clearly defined. This principle remains foundational in Shia jurisprudence for validating forward contracts in trade.
